key_insight: Generative AI makes idea plagiarism harder to define and prove; the paper argues that research-misconduct definitions and institutional practices must be updated to address idea plagiarism when GenAI is involved.
problem_solved: Clarifies the challenge of identifying, defining, and adjudicating plagiarism of ideas in an era where GenAI can generate, remix, or mask the provenance of intellectual contributions, and offers practical policy and procedural guidance.
method: Conceptual and policy analysis of existing plagiarism and research-misconduct definitions in light of GenAI capabilities
Illustrative case scenarios highlighting evidentiary and attribution challenges when GenAI is used
Recommendations for updated definitions, transparency practices, documentation requirements, and institutional safeguards
impact: Equips researchers, journals, and institutions with a framework to update policies and workflows—promoting transparent attribution, better documentation, and fairer adjudication of idea-plagiarism disputes in AI-era research.
visual_elements: Flowchart showing steps for investigating suspected idea plagiarism when GenAI is involved (disclosure → provenance check → evidence assessment → adjudication)
Venn diagram illustrating overlap between human-authored, GenAI-generated, and hybrid ideas to visualize ambiguous ownership
Checklist-style infographic of best practices for researchers and journals (disclose GenAI use, keep drafts/logs, cite prompts/tools, require author attestations)
Timeline or mini-roadmap of recommended policy changes for institutions and publishers
paper_title: Plagiarism of ideas in the age of generative artificial intelligence
